title: Egypt's Pharaohs Return to a Hero's Welcome After Historic World Cup Run
summary: The roar of drums and a sea of red, white, and black flags filled the air outside el-Alamein airport on Friday as Egypt's national soccer team returned from the 2026 World Cup. They didn't bring home the trophy, but they achieved something unprecedented: reaching the knockout stage for the first time in the country's history. Hundreds of supporters, many waving Palestinian flags alongside Egyptian ones, surged around the team's open-top bus for a parade through the coastal city. "We are very happy with the team," fan Mohamed Gehad told AFP. "Their spirit was high, and ours is high as we welcome them." Egypt's campaign was a rollercoaster. They secured their first-ever World Cup victory and then edged Australia in a tense penalty shootout to advance to the last 16. Against defending champions Argentina, they nearly pulled off one of the tournament's great upsets, leading 2-0 with minutes remaining. But Argentina staged a stunning comeback, scoring three late goals to win 3-2. Despite the heartbreak, fans remained jubilant. Handwritten banners read, "You made us proud, men." Captain Mohamed Salah, the former Liverpool forward, wrote on social media: "I'll do everything in my power to ensure this is a new beginning for Egyptian football on the international stage." Coach Hossam Hassan drew both praise and controversy. He waved a Palestinian flag after the Australia win and later called the suffering in Gaza a "shame on the world." The Egyptian Football Association lodged a complaint against the officiating in the Argentina match, accusing referees of injustice—allegations FIFA's refereeing chief Pierluigi Collina dismissed as "unfounded." The players are expected to meet President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi on Saturday. In Gaza, thousands had watched Egypt's matches in makeshift cafes built from salvaged materials. Tragically, Mohammed al-Wahidi, a Palestinian who organized World Cup screenings there, was killed by an Israeli airstrike on the eve of the Argentina match, along with three others, including two siblings aged 10 and 8.
why_it_matters: The story shows how sports can become a stage for national pride and political expression, while also revealing the stark contrast between celebration and the suffering just across the border in Gaza. It forces young people to think about the line between entertainment and real-world crises.

background_read: The 2026 FIFA World Cup was hosted jointly by the United States, Canada, and Mexico. Egypt, a football-mad nation of over 100 million, had previously appeared in the World Cup in 1934, 1990, and 2018 but had never won a match or advanced past the group stage.

This year's run captivated fans at home and in Gaza, a Palestinian territory that has suffered a devastating war and is under an Israeli blockade. The team's captain, Mohamed Salah, is Egypt's all-time leading scorer and a global superstar from his years with Liverpool.

Coach Hossam Hassan's decision to wave a Palestinian flag after the Australia win was a show of solidarity with Palestinians, a gesture that tied sports to one of the world's most volatile conflicts. FIFA’s refereeing chief Pierluigi Collina, an iconic former referee, dismissed the Egyptian complaint about the Argentina match officiating as unfounded.

perspectives.description: Egypt's first-ever knockout stage appearance is a massive morale boost for a country passionate about football. The team's performance unites Egyptians and brings global attention to a growing football power, potentially inspiring more investment in youth sports and national unity.

The coach's Palestinian flag gesture and the federation's complaint against officialling drew criticism and accusations of politicizing the sport. FIFA's dismissal of the allegations suggests Egypt's grievances were seen as a distraction, and the Gaza tragedy highlights the human cost behind the political statement.

This World Cup run fits a pattern: emerging football nations from Africa and the Arab world are closing the gap with traditional powers. However, the overlap of sports and politics is not new – from boycotts to nationalist displays, major tournaments have always amplified geopolitical tensions.

Egypt now has a template for future success. If the country builds on this momentum, it could become a regular contender, but it also must navigate the political minefield that comes with global visibility. The challenge is to keep football a unifying force without getting consumed by regional conflicts.
